```{r}
#| fig-cap: !expr paste0("Forest vertical complexity and internal forest gaps at ", smp("nest cells in available forest"), " nest cells (points) and ", fmt(smp("background cells in available forest"), 0), " background cells in available forest, Clayoquot Sound. Boxes span the middle half of the values, the bar marks the median, and whiskers reach the furthest value within 1.5 box lengths.")
knitr::include_graphics("../03.outputs/figures/F2_structure.png")
```

## Model evaluation

The Clayoquot Sound model discriminated nest cells from background cells no better than chance (@tbl-evaluation). Its AUC was `r fmt(ev("AUC"))` (95 percent CI `r fmt(ev("AUC", "low"))` to `r fmt(ev("AUC", "high"))`), against `r fmt(ev("AUC", m = "desolation"))` for the Desolation Sound model in its own area and `r fmt(ev("AUC", m = "transferred"))` for that model transferred to Clayoquot Sound, and its Boyce index was `r fmt(ev("Boyce index"))` against `r fmt(ev("Boyce index", m = "desolation"))` and `r fmt(ev("Boyce index", m = "transferred"))`. At the training thresholds, `r ev("Nest cells above threshold")` of `r ev("Nest cells")` held-out nest cells and `r fmt(ev("Background cells above threshold"), 0)` of `r fmt(ev("Background cells"), 0)` background cells were classed as nesting habitat, so `r fmt(acc("nest"), 1)` percent of nest cells and `r fmt(acc("background"), 1)` percent of background cells were classed correctly, an average accuracy of `r fmt((acc("nest") + acc("background")) / 2, 1)` percent. The omission error for nests was `r fmt(ev("Omission error, nest"))` and the commission error for nests `r fmt(ev("Commission error, nest"))`, overall accuracy was `r fmt(ev("Overall accuracy"))` (95 percent CI `r fmt(ev("Overall accuracy", "low"))` to `r fmt(ev("Overall accuracy", "high"))`) and kappa `r fmt(ev("Kappa"))` (`r fmt(ev("Kappa", "low"))` to `r fmt(ev("Kappa", "high"))`).

The model did not overfit, its RMSE ratio of `r fmt(ev("RMSE ratio"))` lying below the rejection line of 1.1. The RMSE was `r fmt(ev("RMSE"))`, the mean absolute error `r fmt(ev("MAE"))`, the Brier score `r fmt(ev("Brier score"))` and the relative RMSE `r fmt(ev("Relative RMSE"), 0)`, and Theil's *U* bias of `r fmt(ev("Theil's U bias"))` showed that nearly all of the error was systematic, because predictions averaged `r fmt(ev("Mean prediction"))` while nest cells made up `r fmt(ev("Nest share of cells"), 3)` of all cells. Predictions explained none of the variation in the outcome [*R*² = `r fmt(ev("R2"), 5)`, *F*(`r ev("F statistic", "low")`, `r fmt(ev("F statistic", "high"), 0)`) = `r fmt(ev("F statistic"))`, `r pv(ev("R2", "p_value"))`]. Residuals were spatially autocorrelated [Moran's *I* = `r fmt(ev("Moran's I of residuals"))`, `r pv(ev("Moran's I of residuals", "p_value"))`] but showed no serial correlation along easting [Durbin-Watson = `r fmt(ev("Durbin-Watson"))`, `r pv(ev("Durbin-Watson", "p_value"))`].

```{r}
#| label: tbl-evaluation
#| tbl-cap: "Performance of the Clayoquot Sound model on held-out cells pooled over five spatial folds, beside the Desolation Sound model of Cosgrove et al. (2024) in its own area and transferred to Clayoquot Sound. Intervals are 95% confidence intervals. AUC is the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, RMSE root mean square error and MAE mean absolute error. * P ≤ 0.05, ** P ≤ 0.01, *** P ≤ 0.001, **** P ≤ 0.0001."
show <- c("AUC" = "AUC", "Boyce index" = "Boyce index", "Overall accuracy" = "Overall accuracy", "Kappa" = "Kappa", "Commission error, nest" = "Commission error, nest", "Omission error, nest" = "Omission error, nest", "Commission error, background" = "Commission error, background", "Omission error, background" = "Omission error, background", "R2" = "R²", "RMSE" = "RMSE", "RMSE ratio" = "RMSE ratio", "Relative RMSE" = "Relative RMSE", "MAE" = "MAE", "Brier score" = "Brier score", "Theil's U bias" = "Theil's U bias", "Moran's I of residuals" = "Moran's I of residuals", "Durbin-Watson" = "Durbin-Watson")
tbl("T4_evaluation.csv") |>
  dplyr::filter(metric %in% names(show)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(cell = paste0(dplyr::if_else(metric == "R2", fmt(value, 5), fmt(value)), dplyr::if_else(is.na(low), "", paste0(" (", fmt(low), " to ", fmt(high), ")")), star(p_value))) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(id_cols = metric, names_from = model, values_from = cell, values_fill = "") |>
  dplyr::arrange(match(metric, names(show))) |>
  dplyr::transmute(Measure = show[metric], `Clayoquot Sound, local` = local, `Desolation Sound, own area` = desolation, `Desolation Sound, transferred` = transferred) |>
  flextable::flextable() |> flextable::align(j = 2:4, align = "right", part = "body") |> flextable::align(align = "center", part = "header") |> flextable::set_table_properties(layout = "autofit", width = 1)
```

# Discussion

In Clayoquot Sound, a MaxEnt model rebuilt from `r smp("nest cells in available forest")` local nest cells and open 2019 laser scans ranked held-out nest cells above background cells no more often than chance, and its 95 percent interval on AUC took in both chance and the `r fmt(ev("AUC", m = "transferred"))` reached by the same model transferred from Desolation Sound [@cosgrove2024modeling]. The local model therefore did not outperform the borrowed one, and these data could not show that it did worse. In Oregon a locally selected lidar model also improved little on a transferred one, scoring 0.78 against 0.73 [@hagar2018modeling], but there the transferred model was already adequate on 772 surveyed stands, whereas in Clayoquot Sound the local model had too few nests to learn from, and the Oregon local score may have been measured on the data it was fitted to.

The two measures did not relate to nest sites in Clayoquot Sound as they did in Desolation Sound. Internal forest gaps were larger at nest cells than at background cells, the reverse of the negative relation in the Desolation Sound model [@cosgrove2024modeling], and forest vertical complexity hardly differed. Ground plots at the same Clayoquot Sound nests found shorter and less varied canopy at nests than at random sites, while Desolation Sound nests stood in taller and more varied forest, and both relations differed significantly between the two areas [@silvergieter2011patch]. Nest trees in Clayoquot Sound also stood out less from the trees around them, being taller than available trees by 15 percent of their height against 30 percent in Desolation Sound [@silvergieter2011marbled], a smaller contrast that a 1 ha summary of point heights would be less able to detect. If nest-site selection differed between the two sounds in this way, a model built on Desolation Sound relations would be expected to transfer poorly, as it did, and a model of the same form fitted in Clayoquot Sound would have little to separate.

The background cells may explain much of the weak result, because `r fmt(100 * smp("background cells in available forest") / smp("background cells scanned"), 0)` percent of the scanned background cells met the definition of available forest, so nest cells were compared with forest of much the same kind. Waterhouse et al. [-@waterhouse2009using] found aerial survey ranks failing in Clayoquot Sound for this reason, noting that Clayoquot Sound "has experienced far less habitat loss from logging and has more uniform coverage of suitable forest (Zharikov et al. 2006); consequently a higher proportion of random points might fall within suitable nesting habitat, thereby minimizing the differences between nests and random points" [@waterhouse2009using, 90]. The features that decided which stand a bird used may also have lain beyond a 1 ha summary of point heights. Silvergieter and Lank [-@silvergieter2011patch], whose resource selection functions (RSF) at Clayoquot Sound relied on the density of platform trees, noted that "relative numbers of potential nesting platforms, a key requirement of nesting habitat and an important component of RSF models at Clayoquot Sound, cannot be quantitatively measured by remote methods" [@silvergieter2011patch, 15].

Sample size limited the comparison, because with `r smp("nest cells in available forest")` nest cells spread over five folds the 95 percent interval on AUC spanned `r fmt(ev("AUC", "high") - ev("AUC", "low"))`, and because model residuals were spatially autocorrelated the cells were not independent, so the true uncertainty was likely wider still. Nest positions carried an error of about 50 m within 100 m cells [@cooke2022marbled], and the nests were located 17 to 19 years before the scans were flown, so although cells harvested from 1998 onward were removed, other change in the forest could not be measured. The model's error was almost entirely systematic because MaxEnt output on the complementary log-log scale ranked relative suitability and was not scaled to the small share of nest cells in the sample, so the RMSE, Brier score and *R*² described calibration more than discrimination.

For management in Clayoquot Sound, these results did not support replacing the transferred Desolation Sound model, or the provincial habitat model, which placed 69.4 percent of Clayoquot Sound nests in suitable habitat [@burger2018reliability], with a model fitted to the few local nests. Fitting one model to nests pooled across regions with terms for region, as Silvergieter and Lank [-@silvergieter2011patch] did with ground plots, or measuring individual tall trees from the scans, which formed the model of Lamphear et al. [-@lamphear2025marbled], might draw more from open scans than two stand-level measures, and both could be tested with data already public.

# Conclusion

Open laser scans flown in 2019 and `r smp("nest cells in available forest")` local nest cells were not enough to build a Marbled Murrelet nesting-habitat model for Clayoquot Sound that separated nests from available forest, and the local model could not be shown to improve on the model transferred from Desolation Sound. Until more nests could be located in Clayoquot Sound, the transferred model, or a model fitted to nests pooled across regions, offered the better-supported basis for mapping nesting habitat there.
